## Overview

**bsimms** is an R package for fitting Bayesian stable isotope mixing models
(SIMMs) via Stan, estimating the proportional contribution of two or more
sources to a mixture from tracer data such as stable isotopes. It brings
together mixing-model advances developed across the literature and
implemented in the JAGS-based package MixSIAR --- hierarchical source fitting,
fractionation error, concentration dependence, cross-tracer covariance,
flexible error structures --- and extends them by letting source
proportions depend on an arbitrary lme4-style fixed- and random-effects
formula of mixture-level covariates.

## Installation

You can install the development version of **bsimms** from GitHub like so:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("mattiaghilardi/bsimms")
```

Fitting models also requires a working Stan backend, either
[cmdstanr](https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/) (recommended) or
[rstan](https://mc-stan.org/rstan/), neither of which is installed
automatically:

``` r
# cmdstanr (not on CRAN)
install.packages("cmdstanr", repos = c("https://stan-dev.r-universe.dev", getOption("repos")))
cmdstanr::check_cmdstan_toolchain()
cmdstanr::install_cmdstan()

# or rstan (on CRAN)
Sys.setenv(DOWNLOAD_STATIC_LIBV8 = 1) # only necessary for Linux without the nodejs library / headers
install.packages("rstan", repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org/", dependencies = TRUE)
```

See the [CmdStanR installation
guide](https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/articles/cmdstanr.html) or the
[RStan Getting Started
guide](https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Getting-Started) for
OS-specific instructions and troubleshooting.

## How to use bsimms

As an example, we fit a mixing model to simulated data for a 3-source,
2-isotope model with 10 mixture samples, no covariates (`~1`), raw
replicate source data, and summarised (mean/SD) TDF data.

```{r sim, message = FALSE}
library(bsimms)

sim <- simulate_bsimms_data(
  ~1,
  n_mixture_obs = 10,
  source_names = c("Beaver", "Deer", "Hare"),
  isotope_names = c("d13C", "d15N"),
  seed = 1
)
```

Before fitting, `plot_isospace()` plots the mixtures in isotope space against
the TDF-corrected source means $\pm$ 1 SD, to check that they fall within the
region spanned by the sources.

```{r isospace}
#| fig.alt: >-
#|   Biplot of d13C against d15N showing the ten mixture samples as points
#|   and the Beaver, Deer, and Hare sources as crosshairs of mean plus or
#|   minus one standard deviation; the mixtures lie within the region
#|   spanned by the sources.
#| fig.asp: 0.8
plot_isospace(
  sim$mixture_data,
  sim$source_data,
  sim$tdf_data,
  isotope_names = sim$isotope_names,
  source_means_sds = sim$source_means_sds,
  tdf_means_sds = sim$tdf_means_sds
)
```

```{r fit, message = FALSE, results = "hide"}
fit <- bsimm(
  sim$formula,
  mixture_data = sim$mixture_data,
  source_data = sim$source_data,
  tdf_data = sim$tdf_data,
  isotope_names = sim$isotope_names,
  source_means_sds = sim$source_means_sds,
  tdf_means_sds = sim$tdf_means_sds,
  conc_dep = sim$conc_dep,
  error_structure = sim$error_structure,
  source_col = sim$source_col,
  cores = 4,
  seed = 1
)
```

Printing the fit gives a quick overview of the model.

```{r print-fit}
fit
```

`summary()` reports the population-average source proportions and error
term(s), each with a posterior mean, SD, 95% credible interval, and MCMC
convergence diagnostics (`rhat`, bulk/tail effective sample size). With the
default `error_structure = "process_residual"`, the error term shown per
isotope is `resid_prop`, MixSIAR's multiplicative factor scaling the
source/TDF variance propagated into the mixture -- not a raw residual SD.

```{r summary}
summary(fit)
```

`rhat` close to 1 and large effective sample sizes indicate the chains
mixed well, which we can also check visually with trace and density plots
of the underlying Stan parameters.

```{r plot-fit}
#| fig.alt: "Density and trace plots of p_global and resid_prop across four MCMC chains; densities are unimodal and traces overlap with no trend, indicating good mixing."
#| fig.asp: 1.2
plot(fit)
```

Population-average contributions lean towards Deer and Hare over Beaver,
though with fairly wide credible intervals given the small simulated
sample size.

Since this model has no covariates, every mixture sample shares the same
population-average proportions, so we can visualise their posterior
distribution directly.
  
```{r plot-proportions}
#| fig.alt: "Density plot of posterior source proportions for Beaver, Deer, and Hare; Beaver's distribution is shifted towards lower proportions and more widely spread than the overlapping Deer and Hare distributions."
#| fig.asp: 0.8
p_arr <- posterior_proportions(fit)
plot_proportions(p_arr[, 1, , drop = FALSE], type = "density")
```

## Resources

- [Website](https://mattiaghilardi.github.io/bsimms/): full function
  reference and vignettes.
- [Open an issue](https://github.com/mattiaghilardi/bsimms/issues): report
  a bug or request a feature.
- [Best practices for SIMMs](https://doi.org/10.1139/cjz-2014-0127):
  Phillips et al. (2014) on using stable isotope mixing models
  responsibly in food-web studies.

## Similar packages

**bsimms** sits alongside other R packages for Bayesian stable isotope
mixing models, each with a different scope:

- [MixSIAR](https://github.com/brianstock/MixSIAR): the JAGS-based
  reference implementation **bsimms** reproduces the core modelling
  options of (and extends with an `lme4`-style covariate formula).
- [simmr](https://github.com/andrewcparnell/simmr): fits a restricted
  set of models via JAGS (`simmr_mcmc()`) or, much faster, fixed-form
  variational Bayes (`simmr_ffvb()`).
- [cosimmr](https://github.com/emmagovan/cosimmr): simmr's
  variational-Bayes approach extended to continuous covariates.
- [MixMustR](https://open-aims.github.io/MixMustR/): jointly fits tracer
  data (e.g. stable isotopes, fatty acids) and independent
  source-composition data (e.g. eDNA metabarcoding) via two linked
  likelihoods, with an optional unsampled-source component relaxing the
  sum-to-1 constraint.

## Citing bsimms and related software

When using **bsimms**, please cite it as follows:

- Ghilardi M (YEAR). bsimms: Bayesian Stable Isotope Mixing Models using
  'Stan'. R package version XXX.
  <https://github.com/mattiaghilardi/bsimms>.

The same information can be obtained by running `citation("bsimms")`.

As **bsimms** generates and fits Stan programs, please additionally
cite Stan:

Carpenter, B., Gelman, A., Hoffman, M.D., Lee, D., Goodrich, B.,
Betancourt, M., Brubaker, M., Guo, J., Li, P., & Riddell, A. (2017).
Stan: A probabilistic programming language. *Journal of Statistical
Software*, 76(1), 1-32. <doi:10.18637/jss.v076.i01>

See <https://mc-stan.org/about/#citing-stan> for Stan's own up-to-date
citation guidance.

Please also cite whichever backend you used to fit the model, the R
interface actually compiling and sampling from the Stan program:

```r
citation("cmdstanr") # if backend = "cmdstanr" (the default, if installed)
citation("rstan")    # if backend = "rstan"
```

More generally, bsimms depends on R itself and on many other R
packages; use the `citation` function to find out how to cite each of
them.

If you use `plot_proportions()`, `plot_isospace()`, or
`plot()`/`print()` on a `conditional_effects()` result, please also
consider citing **ggplot2**. If you use `plot()`/`pp_check()` on the
fitted model itself, please consider citing **bayesplot**. If you use
`loo()`/`waic()`/`loo_compare()`, please consider citing **loo**. All
three provide the underlying implementation for these functions.
